questions.question: Distinguish scarcity from a shortage, define opportunity cost precisely, and read every position on, inside and beyond the production possibility curve.
questions.expected_answer: Scarcity is the permanent condition of limited resources against unlimited wants, present in every economy and never solved; a shortage is a temporary, fixable market condition where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. Opportunity cost is the value of the single NEXT BEST alternative sacrificed — not everything forgone, only the top alternative walked away from. On the PPC: a point ON the curve is full, efficient use of resources; a point INSIDE the curve is underutilisation — idle workers and machines, as with South Africa's unemployment above thirty percent; a point BEYOND the curve is unattainable with current resources; and the whole curve shifts outward when resources grow or technology improves, which is economic growth. The curve's downward slope expresses opportunity cost: more of one product means surrendering some of the other.

questions.question: Describe the circular flow with its leakages and injections, and state the GDP and GNI counting rules with the limitations of the totals.
questions.expected_answer: Households sell factors of production to firms on the factor market and receive income; firms sell goods and services back on the product market — money circulating one way, goods and factors the other. Leakages drain the flow: saving, taxation and spending on imports. Injections refill it: investment, government spending and export earnings. Injections above leakages expand the flow; leakages above injections contract it. GDP is the market value of all FINAL goods and services produced WITHIN the borders in a year — the where rule, so a foreign-owned plant in Gqeberha counts; final goods only, or intermediate inputs like the potatoes in the fish-and-chips parcel are double-counted. GNI follows the who rule: income of the nation's factor owners, adding earnings abroad and subtracting what foreign owners remit home. Per capita versions allow comparison, but the totals miss unpaid household work, much informal activity, the distribution of income and environmental damage.

questions.question: State the laws of demand and supply, explain movement versus shift with an example, and name the four phases of the business cycle with the three indicator classes.
questions.expected_answer: Law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal — a downward-sloping curve. Law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises — an upward-sloping curve. Their crossing is equilibrium: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, no surplus, no shortage. Only the product's own price causes movement along a curve; anything else — income, tastes, related prices, buyer numbers, input costs, technology, weather — shifts the whole curve. Example: avian flu shifts egg supply left, a shortage opens at the old price, the price is bid up, and the new equilibrium has a higher price and smaller quantity — four steps: which curve, which direction, which excess, which new equilibrium. Business cycle phases in fixed order: recovery, prosperity, recession, depression. Indicators: leading, such as building plans approved, turn before the economy; coincident, such as current retail sales, move with it; lagging, such as unemployment, confirm the turn afterwards.
